c.tagline: Lagoon-side capital of commerce where zemidjan motorcycles and Voodoo tradition rule the streets.

taxi.color: green and yellow (shared taxis) / unmarked private cars
taxi.fareNote: Fares are negotiated before boarding, not metered; shared taxis run fixed routes for a set per-seat price while private hires are haggled.

emergency.note: Fire/Sapeurs-pompiers: 118. Response times can be slow outside central districts; hotels and tour operators often keep direct lines to trusted clinics.

hood_landmark.Haie Vive: Sofitel Cotonou Marina Hotel & Spa, Cotonou

avoid.reason: Avoid the Dantokpa Market area and the beaches (including Plage de Cotonou) after dark, where muggings and robberies are a known risk.
Pickpocketing is common in Dantokpa Market and on crowded zémidjan (motorbike taxi) routes; keep phones out of sight in traffic.

hood_desc: Cotonou's leafy diplomatic and expat quarter, home to embassies, upscale villas and the city's top hotels; suits business travelers and those wanting comfort and security.
Beachfront strip with direct Atlantic Ocean access and a lively scene of open-air seafood restaurants and bars; suits travelers wanting a laid-back coastal base with nightlife nearby.
Convenient district right by the airport, useful for short layovers or early flights, though it has fewer sightseeing draws than other areas.
Downtown core anchored by the sprawling Dantokpa Market, government offices and colonial-era streets; suits travelers who want to be in the thick of city life on a budget.
Sprawling residential district east of the lagoon bridge, popular with long-stay visitors, volunteers and NGO workers seeking an authentic, less touristy base at lower prices.
lodging: Best Western Plus Nobila Airport Hotel

water.note: Tap water is unsafe for tourists; use bottled water.

transit.pay: City buses use a rechargeable card obtainable at Dantokpa Market and major stops; most visitors instead pay cash directly to zemidjan and taxi drivers, or pay in-app via Gozem/Yango for fixed, cashless fares. Small XOF bills are essential since drivers rarely carry change.
transit.hours: Zemidjan and taxis operate roughly 6am-11pm with reduced night availability; formal buses run daytime hours only and service outside the city center thins out after dark.
transit.note: There is no metro, tram or regular passenger rail in Cotonou; getting around is dominated by zemidjan moto-taxis, shared minibuses and a limited SOTRACOB bus network.

air: Cardinal Bernardin Gantin International Airport / Cadjehoun Airport (COO)
bus: Long-distance bush taxis/minibuses from Gare Jonquet to Ouidah, Porto-Novo, Parakou and beyond
ferry: Pirogue (canoe) crossings on Lake Nokoué to the stilt village of Ganvié - tourist/local use, no fixed schedule

airport.name: Cadjehoun Airport (Cardinal Bernardin Gantin International Airport) - COO
airport.drive: 15-25 min depending on traffic (airport sits within city limits near Fidjrossè/Cadjehoun)

transit.m: Official airport taxi rank to city center (~20 min)
Zemidjan moto-taxi just outside terminal gate (~15 min, luggage limited)
Gozem/Yango app-hailed ride (pickup a short walk from arrivals)

tip.r: Tipping is not customary or expected, though rounding up for good restaurant service or hotel porters is appreciated.

food.name: Amiwo
food.desc: Benin's celebration dish: cornmeal paste cooked in a red tomato, pepper and palm-oil sauce until stained orange, served with chicken or grilled fish.

places.name: Maquis du Port
places.note: Waterside maquis pairing amiwo with grilled barracuda, the classic Cotonou combination.

places.name: Le Lieu Unique
places.note: Sit-down restaurant doing polished versions of Beninese staples including amiwo.

places.name: Dantokpa Market food stalls
places.note: West Africa's biggest market; cooks ladle amiwo from huge pots at lunchtime for pocket change.

food.name: Akassa with Fried Fish
food.desc: Sour fermented maize dough steamed in leaves, eaten with the fingers alongside fried or stewed fish in a peppery tomato sauce.

places.name: Dantokpa Market food stalls
places.note: Leaf-wrapped akassa sold by the bundle and eaten on the spot with fish sauce.

places.name: Fidjrosse Beach maquis
places.note: The beach road is a run of open-air maquis grilling and frying the day's catch.

places.name: Les Nouveaux Alizes
places.note: Seaside spot serving local staples with fish in a calmer setting than the markets.

food.name: Ablo
food.desc: Soft, slightly sweet steamed rice or maize cakes, spongy and white, used to mop up fish and pepper sauces or eaten as a snack.

places.name: Dantokpa Market food stalls
places.note: Vendors stack fresh ablo in baskets from early morning; buy a few with sauce.

places.name: Maquis du Port
places.note: Serves ablo as the starch alongside grilled fish and pepper sauce.

places.name: Haie Vive maquis
places.note: The expat-friendly quarter's small maquis keep ablo on the daily rotation.

food.name: Atassi
food.desc: Rice and black-eyed beans cooked together into a soft, savoury one-pot, usually topped with tomato sauce and fried plantain.

places.name: Dantokpa Market food stalls
places.note: The cheapest and most authentic bowl of atassi in the city, served all day.

places.name: Fidjrosse Beach maquis
places.note: Casual beach kitchens plate atassi with aloko and grilled fish.

places.name: Le Lieu Unique
places.note: Restaurant take on Beninese one-pot dishes for those who want table service.

food.name: Wagasi Cheese
food.desc: Fulani cow's-milk cheese from northern Benin, firm and squeaky, fried in palm oil until golden and eaten in sauce or on skewers.

places.name: Dantokpa Market food stalls
places.note: Wagasi sold fresh by northern traders and fried to order at nearby stalls.

places.name: Haie Vive maquis
places.note: Fried wagasi is a standard beer snack at the quarter's evening maquis.

places.name: Maquis du Port
places.note: Offers wagasi among its Beninese starters alongside grilled fish.

food.name: Grilled Barracuda
food.desc: Whole Atlantic barracuda or capitaine scored, marinated and grilled over charcoal, served with piment sauce, onions and fried plantain.

places.name: Fidjrosse Beach maquis
places.note: Charcoal grills line the beach road; pick your fish from the ice and wait with a beer.

places.name: Maquis du Port
places.note: Long-running waterfront maquis known for grilled barracuda with amiwo.

places.name: Les Nouveaux Alizes
places.note: Sea breeze, cold drinks and whole grilled fish off the Atlantic.

food.name: Sodabi
food.desc: Benin's national spirit, distilled from palm wine and drunk neat in small glasses, sometimes infused with pineapple, ginger or bitter herbs.

places.name: Dantokpa Market
places.note: Traders sell plain and infused sodabi in recycled bottles at the market's drinks aisles.

places.name: Fidjrosse Beach maquis
places.note: Every beach maquis keeps a bottle of flavoured sodabi behind the counter.

places.name: Haie Vive maquis
places.note: Evening bars in the quarter pour sodabi shots alongside cold Beninoise beer.

food.name: Tchakpalo
food.desc: Cloudy, lightly fermented sorghum or millet beer, tart and low in alcohol, ladled from calabashes at roadside stalls across southern Benin.

places.name: Dantokpa Market
places.note: Women sell tchakpalo by the calabash near the market's food sections.

places.name: Fidjrosse Beach maquis
places.note: Served cold alongside grilled fish; ask for it fresh rather than day-old.

places.name: Jonquet street stalls
places.note: Nightlife quarter where street vendors sell tchakpalo and bissap into the evening.

landmarks: Notre-Dame de Miséricorde Cathedral
Painted in bold red-and-white stripes, this striking Catholic cathedral in the heart of Cotonou is one of the city's most photographed and colorful landmarks.
Ganvié Stilt Village
Nicknamed the Venice of Africa, this remarkable lake village built entirely on stilts over Lake Nokoué is reachable only by canoe and ranks among Benin's top attractions.
Dantokpa Market
One of West Africa's largest open-air markets, this sprawling, chaotic bazaar overflows with textiles, voodoo fetishes, and spices, offering an unforgettable sensory experience.
Fondation Zinsou
Africa's first private contemporary art foundation, this free gallery in Cotonou showcases works by celebrated African artists in a striking modern exhibition space.
Place de l'Étoile Rouge
This landmark roundabout, crowned by a red star monument from Benin's Marxist-era history, serves as a memorable photo stop and central orientation point in the city.
Cotonou Beach
The city's palm-fringed Atlantic shoreline draws locals and visitors alike for sunset strolls, fresh seafood shacks, and views of colorful fishing pirogues.
Cotonou Friendship Bridge (Pont du Novotel)
This modern cable-stayed bridge spanning the Cotonou lagoon has become an emblem of the city's growth and offers striking illuminated views at night.
Stade de l'Amitié
Benin's largest stadium hosts national football matches and major concerts, standing as a proud symbol of the country's sporting culture on the outskirts of Cotonou.
Musée de la Fondation Zinsou Ouidah Route (Route des Esclaves gateway)
Just outside Cotonou, this historic corridor traces the somber path enslaved Africans once walked to the coast, marked by moving memorial sculptures.
Cotonou Central Mosque
A prominent minareted mosque serving the city's large Muslim community, its domes and towers form a distinctive part of the Cotonou skyline.

train.note: Benin has no working passenger rail service. The old OCBN Cotonou-Parakou line no longer carries scheduled passengers and the planned Cotonou-Niamey railway was never completed. Travel overland by long-distance coach instead.

bus.note: Coaches leave from the operators' terminals in central Cotonou. ABC Transport runs the daily Lagos-Cotonou-Lome-Accra coastal corridor. Carry your passport and CFA/Naira cash for the Nigeria, Togo and Ghana land borders. For Niamey (Niger) and Ouagadougou, regional lines also operate.

ferry.note: No scheduled international passenger ferries; the Port of Cotonou is cargo only. Locally, motorized pirogues cross Lake Nokoue to the stilt village of Ganvie.
